title: Running and Debugging Applications
description: Learn how to run ASP.NET Core applications from the CLI and debug them with breakpoints, watch windows, and the built-in logger. Covers Visual Studio and VS Code debugging workflows.

blocks.text: Running your application is only the first step. **Debugging** — finding and fixing issues in your code — is where you really understand how your application works. ASP.NET Core provides excellent debugging support in both Visual Studio and VS Code, with breakpoints, variable inspection, and integrated logging.

In this lesson, you will learn how to run your app with debugging enabled, set breakpoints to pause execution, inspect variables, and use the built-in logging system to understand what your application is doing.
To run your application in debug mode, use the `dotnet run` command. In Visual Studio or VS Code, you can also press F5 (or the green "Run" button) to launch with the debugger attached automatically.

blocks.title: Running with the .NET CLI debugger
blocks.content: Use the dotnet run command to launch the app with the debugger attached.

blocks.text: When you run with the debugger attached, you can set **breakpoints** — markers that pause execution at a specific line of code. When execution pauses, you can inspect variables, step through code line by line, and understand the flow of your application.

A breakpoint tells the debugger: "Stop here so I can see what is happening." You set a breakpoint by clicking in the gutter (the left margin) next to a line of code, or by pressing F9 on that line. When execution reaches the breakpoint, the application pauses, and you can inspect the current state.

blocks.title: Debugging actions
items: **Set breakpoint** — Click in the gutter next to a line, or press F9
**Continue** — Press F5 to resume execution until the next breakpoint
**Step Over** — Press F10 to execute the current line and move to the next
**Step Into** — Press F11 to enter a method call and debug inside it
**Step Out** — Press Shift+F11 to finish the current method and return to the caller
**Inspect variables** — Hover over variables or use the Locals/Watch windows

blocks.title: Conditional breakpoints
blocks.text: Right-click a breakpoint and choose "Conditions" to pause only when a specific condition is true. For example, pause only when `product.Id == 5`. This saves time when debugging loops or repeated requests.

Visual Studio offers the most comprehensive debugging experience. The Locals window shows all variables in the current scope, the Autos window shows recently used variables, and the Watch window lets you monitor specific expressions. The Call Stack window shows the chain of method calls that led to the current point.

blocks.title: Debugging a controller action
blocks.content: Set a breakpoint inside a controller action and inspect the incoming request data.

blocks.text: VS Code debugging uses a `launch.json` configuration file. The C# Dev Kit extension creates this file automatically when you first press F5. The debugging experience is similar to Visual Studio, with a Run panel at the top showing step controls.

blocks.title: launchSettings.json profiles
blocks.text: The `Properties/launchSettings.json` file defines named launch profiles. Each profile specifies the URL, SSL port, and environment. You can add multiple profiles (e.g., one for HTTP, one for HTTPS) and select which one to use when debugging.

In addition to the debugger, ASP.NET Core includes a powerful logging system that writes messages to the console, debug output, and other providers. Logging is essential for understanding what your application does in production, where breakpoints are not available.

blocks.title: Logging in a controller
blocks.content: Inject ILogger into a controller and write structured log messages at different severity levels.

blocks.title: Log levels in order of severity
items: **Trace** — Very detailed diagnostic information, typically disabled in production
**Information** — General application flow and milestone events
**Warning** — Unexpected events that are not errors but deserve attention
**Error** — Failures in the current operation that do not stop the application
**Critical** — Severe failures that require immediate attention

blocks.title: What to debug and when
items: **NullReferenceException** — Set a breakpoint on the line before the crash and inspect variables to find which object is null
**Wrong data in a view** — Set a breakpoint in the controller action and inspect the model before it is passed to the view
**Form not submitting** — Set a breakpoint in the POST action and check if `ModelState.IsValid` is false
**Route not found (404)** — Check the route pattern in Program.cs and verify the URL matches the expected format
**Database query returns nothing** — Set a breakpoint and inspect the LINQ query or SQL generated by EF Core

items.text: A breakpoint was set in a controller action
items.hint: Click the gutter next to a line of code to add a red dot breakpoint marker

items.text: The application was run in debug mode (F5 or `dotnet run`)
items.hint: Make sure the debugger is attached, not just the app running

items.text: A variable was inspected during a paused breakpoint
items.hint: Hover over a variable or check the Locals/Watch window

items.text: Logging output was visible in the terminal or Output window
items.hint: Look for Information or Warning messages when triggering the logged action

items.text: A log level was changed in appsettings.json
items.hint: Set "Default" to "Debug" under "Logging" to see more detailed output

terms.definition: A marker placed on a line of code that pauses execution when the debugger reaches it, allowing you to inspect variables and application state.
The built-in logging interface in ASP.NET Core. Supports structured logging at six severity levels from Trace to Critical.
A .NET feature that applies code changes to a running application without restarting. Available automatically in .NET 6+.
A tool (built into Visual Studio and VS Code) that lets you pause, step through, and inspect running code to understand its behavior and find bugs.

blocks.title: Debug a Controller Action
blocks.description: Set up debugging in your project and use breakpoints and logging to inspect a running request.
steps: Open the `Controllers/HomeController.cs` file in your MyFirstApp project
Set a breakpoint on the line inside the `Index()` action method (the first line after the method declaration)
Run the app in debug mode by pressing F5 in your editor
Open a browser and navigate to the home page URL
When execution pauses at the breakpoint, inspect the controller instance and any available properties in the Locals window
Add a `_logger.LogInformation` call at the start of the `Index()` method and confirm the log message appears in the terminal or Output window
Remove the breakpoint and stop the debug session
blocks.expectedOutcome: The application pauses at the breakpoint when navigating to the home page. The logger outputs an Information-level message to the terminal. You can see the controller and logger instances in the debugging windows.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Use F5 (or `dotnet run`) to launch your app with the debugger attached
Set breakpoints by clicking the gutter or pressing F9 to pause execution and inspect state
Step Over (F10), Step Into (F11), and Step Out (Shift+F11) let you navigate through code execution
Conditional breakpoints only pause when a specific condition is true, saving time in loops
ILogger provides structured logging at six severity levels: Trace through Critical
Log levels are controlled in appsettings.json and can be changed without modifying code
blocks.takeaway: Debugging is not just about fixing errors — it is your primary tool for understanding how your ASP.NET Core application processes requests. Master breakpoints and logging early, and they will serve you throughout your entire career.
